A star died. From its ashes, a planet may have been born.
The star, a white dwarf, sits 270 light-years away.
Hubble recorded its light in 1999. A hundred spectral lines went unidentified.
This year, an astronomer rechecked them. Many matched niobium.
Niobium, zinc, copper: elements heavier than iron, made in dying stars.
A planet born with its star would be rich in silicon and iron. This had almost none.
A dying red giant shed its layers, and the debris collapsed into a gas giant.
TESS then saw a signal repeating every four point four days: a Jupiter-sized world, closer than Mercury is to the Sun.
The star's heat strips its air, and the debris falls back, carrying the planet's chemistry to Hubble.
Still only a candidate. Could our Sun's ashes do this too? Latoon. Voyaging the unseen. Follow for more.
